rows.significance: Earliest hadith-fiqh compilation with qirad (mudarabah) chapter.
rows.detail_long: Malik ibn Anas (93-179 AH, 712-795 CE) was the imam of Medina and the founder of the Maliki school of law. He was born in Medina and lived his whole life there. He worked on the Muwatta for forty years, and its hadith are arranged by legal topic. Many scholars transmitted the book from him, and it has been printed in two transmissions, one by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani and one by Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi. The printed text is divided into sixty-one books. It opens with prayer and purification, and its commercial part includes the Book of Sales (Kitab al-Buyu'), the Book of Qirad (Kitab al-Qirad), the Book of Musaqah (Kitab al-Musaqah), the Book of Renting Land (Kitab Kira' al-Ard) and the Book of Pre-emption (Kitab al-Shuf'ah). Source: contents list and author note for the edition corrected and numbered by Muhammad Fu'ad Abd al-Baqi (Dar Ihya' al-Turath al-Arabi, Beirut, 1985), as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.detail_long: Abu Yusuf Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim al-Ansari (113-182 AH, 731-798 CE) was the companion and student of Abu Hanifa and the first to spread his school. He was born in Kufa, served as judge in Baghdad under the caliphs al-Mahdi, al-Hadi and al-Rashid, and was the first to be called 'judge of judges'. Kitab al-Kharaj opens by saying that this is what Abu Yusuf wrote to the Commander of the Faithful Harun al-Rashid. In the preface he says the caliph asked him to write a comprehensive book to act on in collecting the kharaj, the tithes ('ushur), the alms (sadaqat) and the jawali, and that the caliph's aim was to lift injustice from his subjects. The top level of the contents list shows the author's introduction, a chapter on dividing spoils taken from the enemy, and a chapter on increase, decrease and loss in zakat. Source: author's preface and contents list of the edition edited by Taha Abd al-Ra'uf Sa'd and Sa'd Hasan Muhammad (al-Maktaba al-Azhariyya lil-Turath), as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.significance: Foundational Shafi'i corpus incl. sale/lease.
rows.detail_long: Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i (150-204 AH, 767-820 CE) was born in Gaza in Palestine and taken to Mecca as a small child. He memorised the Qur'an at seven and Malik's Muwatta at ten, and learned Malik's law from Malik himself. The library description says al-Shafi'i dictated al-Umm to his students in Egypt, giving the opinions he reached at the end of his life, known as his 'new school'. It says he opens the books and chapters with a verse or a hadith that he treats as the basis for the rulings that follow, and that he takes the Qur'an and Sunnah as the basis for deriving rulings and turns to analogy and reasoning when he finds no text. The contents list includes the Book of Sales (Kitab al-Buyu'), a chapter on salaf, the Book of Pledge (Kitab al-Rahn), and sections on bankruptcy, settlement, transfer of debt, guarantee, partnership and agency, followed by qirad, musaqah, muzara'ah, and hire and land rent (al-Ijarah wa Kira' al-Ard). Source: book description and contents list of the Dar al-Fikr, Beirut edition (second printing, 1983, eight parts), as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.significance: Core Maliki transactions law.
rows.detail_long: The library record names the author of al-Mudawwana as Malik ibn Anas al-Asbahi of Medina (died 179 AH, 795 CE) and classes the book as Maliki law. Its description says the Mudawwana gathers the opinions transmitted from Imam Malik and those derived on his principles, with opinions of some of his companions and some reports and hadith on questions of Maliki law. It says the work ranks in value after Malik's Muwatta, that the scholars of Qayrawan relied on it for fatwa, and that it is made up of questions and answers on points of law, numbering 6,200 and arranged by the chapters of fiqh. The same description says Sahnun was the first to explain and arrange it, and the author note says Sahnun al-Tanukhi compiled it. The contents list includes the Book of Currency Exchange (Kitab al-Sarf), three books on salam, the Book of Deferred Terms (Kitab al-Ajal), Invalid Sales, Murabahah, Gharar, Agencies, Ju'l and Hire, Musaqah, Partnership (Kitab al-Sharikah) and Qirad. Source: book description and contents list of the Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya edition (first printing, 1994, four parts), as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.significance: Early fiscal/economic treatise.
rows.detail_long: Abu Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam (157-224 AH, 774-838 CE) was one of the leading scholars of hadith, literature and law. He came from Herat, where he was born and educated, served as judge in Tarsus for eighteen years, and died in Mecca after the pilgrimage. The library description of Kitab al-Amwal says it is one of the books that speak about the Islamic economic system and its foundations, meaning the revenues of the public treasury such as kharaj, zakat and jizya and their rulings, and how these funds are spent, and it calls the book an early treatment of these subjects. It says the book holds 1,327 reports with chains of transmission arranged in eight books, beginning with the Book of Fay' and ending with the Book of Sadaqah, by which the author means zakat. In each chapter he gives the Prophet's hadith first, then the sayings of the Companions and Successors, then his own understanding. Section titles in the contents list include the Book of the Fifth (Kitab al-Khums) and its rulings, and a book on the rulings of lands: their grant, revival, reserves and waters. Source: book description and contents list of the edition edited by Khalil Muhammad Harras (Dar al-Fikr, Beirut), as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

The contents list includes the Book of Partnership (Kitab al-Sharikah), the Book of Sales (Kitab al-Buyu'), Currency Exchange (al-Sarf), Hire (al-Ijarat), Guarantee (al-Kafalah), Pledge (al-Rahn), Mudarabah and Muzara'ah. rows.detail_long: Ala' al-Din Abu Bakr ibn Mas'ud al-Kasani (died 587 AH, 1191 CE) was a Hanafi jurist of Aleppo, where he died. The library description says Bada'i' al-Sana'i' fi Tartib al-Shara'i' is a commentary on Tuhfat al-Fuqaha' by al-Samarqandi, but that al-Kasani blended the original text with the commentary and gave his book a new legal arrangement of its own. It says the book is arranged by the chapters of fiqh, is marked by method, clarity and good order, and compares Hanafi law with other views, especially the Shafi'i school: it states the Hanafi ruling, gives the opposing view and its evidence, then returns to the Hanafi evidence. The description counts it among the relied-upon books of the Hanafi school. The contents list includes the Book of Hire (Kitab al-Ijarah), the Book of Istisna', the Book of Sales (Kitab al-Buyu'), Guarantee (al-Kafalah), Transfer of Debt (al-Hawalah), Agency (al-Wakalah), Partnership (al-Sharikah), Mudarabah and Pledge (al-Rahn). rows.detail_long: Abu al-Walid Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Rushd of Cordoba (520-595 AH, 1126-1198 CE), known as Ibn Rushd the Grandson, was a Maliki and a philosopher whom Europeans call Averroes; he is called 'the Grandson' to tell him apart from his grandfather of the same name. The library record classes Bidayat al-Mujtahid wa Nihayat al-Muqtasid as comparative law. Its description says it is one of the most important books on juristic disagreement: though small in size, it holds the main questions of fiqh, showing where the jurists agree and differ, explaining the positions of the different schools, giving the scholars' views on each question and discussing the opinions and evidence without partisanship. The contents list includes the Book of Sales (Kitab al-Buyu'), Currency Exchange (al-Sarf), Salam, Murabahah Sale, Hire (al-Ijarat), Ju'l, Qirad, Musaqah, Partnership (al-Sharikah), Pledges (al-Ruhun), Guarantee (al-Kafalah), Transfer of Debt (al-Hawalah) and Agency (al-Wakalah). rows.detail_long: Muwaffaq al-Din Abu Muhammad Abdullah ibn Qudama (541-620 AH, 1146-1223 CE) was a jurist and one of the senior Hanbalis. The library description calls al-Mughni a huge encyclopedia of law in the Hanbali school and in comparative law, written as a commentary on the short manual of al-Khiraqi and arranged by the chapters and questions of fiqh. It says he explains each question, follows it with similar questions and rulings, widens the evidence, records the positions of the jurists, shows where there is consensus, and prefers what he finds strongest in evidence. The contents list includes the Book of Sales (Kitab al-Buyu'), Pledge (al-Rahn), the Bankrupt (al-Muflis), Settlement (al-Sulh), Transfer of Debt (al-Hawalah), Guarantee (al-Daman), Partnership (al-Sharikah), Agency (al-Wakalah), Musaqah and Hire (al-Ijarat). rows.significance: Ethics of earning/trade; maqasid roots.
rows.detail_long: Abu Hamid Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Ghazali al-Tusi (450-505 AH, 1058-1111 CE), called Hujjat al-Islam, was a philosopher, a Sufi and one of the senior Shafi'i jurists, with about two hundred works. He was born and died at Tabaran, the chief town of Tus in Khurasan, and travelled to Nishapur, Baghdad, the Hijaz, Syria and Egypt before returning home. The library description calls Ihya' Ulum al-Din the fastest-spreading and most famous of Sufi writings, and records that readers took three positions on it: those who warned against it, those who exalted it, and those who called for it to be corrected. The contents list divides the work into four quarters: acts of worship, customs, destructive matters and saving matters. Within it al-Ghazali sets out the proprieties of trades, crafts and kinds of earning in five chapters: the merit of earning; knowing valid sale, purchase and dealings; justice in dealing; doing good in dealing; and the merchant's care for himself and his religion. Source: book description, contents list and text of the Dar al-Ma'rifa, Beirut edition (four parts), as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.detail_long: Taqi al-Din Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Abd al-Halim Ibn Taymiyya (661-728 AH, 1263-1328 CE) was born in Harran and taken by his father to Damascus, where he became famous. He was imprisoned more than once and died a prisoner in the citadel of Damascus. Majmu' al-Fatawa is a collection of his writings gathered and arranged by Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn Qasim, helped by his son Muhammad. The library description calls it one of the largest relied-upon encyclopedias of the religious sciences, covering creed, theology, logic, law and its principles, Qur'an commentary, hadith and Sufism. The contents list gives one subject to each volume: the first volumes cover creed, volumes 13 to 17 Qur'an commentary, volume 18 hadith, volumes 19 and 20 legal theory, and volumes 21 to 35 law. Within the law volumes, volume 29 is titled Sale (al-Bay'), volume 30 Settlement to Lost Property, and volume 31 Endowment (al-Waqf) to Manumission. Source: edition card and contents list of the King Fahd Complex for the Printing of the Holy Qur'an edition (Medina, 2004), as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.detail_long: Shams al-Din Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, known as Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya (691-751 AH, 1292-1350 CE), was born and died in Damascus. He was a student of Ibn Taymiyya, edited his books and spread his learning, and was imprisoned with him in the citadel of Damascus. The library description says I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in an Rabb al-Alamin is a book that joins law, legal theory, the objectives of the Shari'ah, the history of legislation and governance according to the Shari'ah. It says he urges following the Prophet's reports, sets out the sources of legislation, and explains the letter of Umar to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari on judging. He then studies in detail some legal and theoretical topics such as riba, blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i'), legal devices (hiyal), analogy, the conditions of the mufti and the manners of giving fatwa. The book ends with long sections on the Prophet's own fatwas, arranged by the chapters of fiqh. Source: book description and contents list of the Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya, Beirut edition edited by Muhammad Abd al-Salam Ibrahim (1991, four parts), as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.detail_long: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Habib al-Mawardi (364-450 AH, 974-1058 CE) was a leading Shafi'i jurist who grew up in Basra, served as a judge, and was given the title Aqda al-Qudat in 429 AH. The author note describes him as one of the prominent political figures of the Abbasid state. The library record gives the full title as al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyya wa al-Wilayat al-Diniyya and classes it under governance according to the Shari'ah. Its description says the book deals with the Islamic political, financial, judicial, administrative and military systems: the rules of the imamate and caliphate, the vizierate, governorships, the judiciary, the court of grievances and the hisbah, and the rulings of fay', jizya, kharaj and the revival of dead land. Chapter titles in the contents list include chapter 11 on the administration of alms (sadaqat), chapter 13 on imposing jizya and kharaj, chapter 15 on reviving dead land and bringing out water, chapter 17 on land grants (iqta') and chapter 18 on setting up the diwan. Source: book description and contents list of the Dar al-Hadith, Cairo edition, as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.significance: First codification of Hanafi civil/contract law.
rows.detail_long: The library record gives the author of Majallat al-Ahkam al-Adliyya as a committee made up of a number of scholars and jurists in the Ottoman caliphate. A note about the Majalla printed at the front of the text says it is a body of legislation made up of sixteen books, the first being the Book of Sales and the last the Book of Judgeship, and that each book treats one subject and is divided into chapters, each chapter into sections. The same note describes it as the first setting-down of Islamic law in the civil field in the form of legal articles, on the school of Imam Abu Hanifa. The contents list names the sixteen books: Sales (al-Buyu'), Hire (al-Ijarat), Guarantee (al-Kafalah), Transfer of Debt (al-Hawalah), Pledge (al-Rahn), Trusts (al-Amanat), Gift (al-Hibah), Usurpation and Destruction, Interdiction, Permission, Duress and Pre-emption, Companies (al-Sharikat), Agency (al-Wakalah), Settlement and Release, Acknowledgement, Claims, Evidence and Oath-taking, and Judgeship (al-Qada'). Source: edition card, front note and contents list of the edition edited by Najib Hawawini (Nur Muhammad, Karkhana Tijarat-i Kutub, Karachi), as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.detail_long: Burhan al-Din Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Abi Bakr al-Marghinani (511-593 AH, 1117-1197 CE), known as 'the author of the Hidayah', was one of the senior Hanafi jurists. His name refers to Marghinan, in the region of Farghana. A library description says al-Hidayah is the best-known book and most important short manual of law on the Hanafi school. It explains that the Hidayah is itself a commentary on al-Marghinani's own Bidayat al-Mubtadi, in which he combined the manual of al-Quduri with al-Jami' al-Saghir of Muhammad ibn al-Hasan; he first wrote a long commentary called Kifayat al-Muntahi and, finding it large, wrote a shorter one named al-Hidayah Sharh Bidayat al-Mubtadi. The contents list includes the Book of Partnership (Kitab al-Sharikah), Endowment (al-Waqf), Sales (al-Buyu'), Currency Exchange (al-Sarf), Guarantee (al-Kafalah), Transfer of Debt (al-Hawalah), Agency (al-Wakalah), Mudarabah, Deposit (al-Wadi'ah) and Hire (al-Ijarat). Source: edition card and contents list of the Dar Ihya' al-Turath al-Arabi, Beirut edition (2004, four parts), and the description printed with its commentary Fath al-Qadir, both as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.significance: Maliki primer with transactions.
rows.detail_long: Abu Muhammad Abdullah ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani (310-386 AH, 922-996 CE) was a Maliki scholar who was called 'the little Malik'. The author note quotes al-Qadi Iyad as saying that he summarised the school and filled the lands with his writings, and that he studied under the jurists of Qayrawan. Among his works it lists an abridgement of the Mudawwana and 'the famous Risalah', which some said he wrote at the age of seventeen. The text of the Risalah is a short work of 170 printed pages arranged in chapters. The contents list opens with a chapter on what tongues utter and hearts believe of the obligatory matters of religion, then moves through purification, prayer, fasting and the other acts of worship. Later chapters include one titled 'on sales and what resembles sales' (Bab fi al-Buyu' wa ma Shakala al-Buyu') and one on judgments and testimonies. rows.significance: Hanbali source naming tawarruq.
rows.detail_long: Mansur ibn Yunus al-Buhuti (1000-1051 AH, 1591-1641 CE) was the leading Hanbali scholar of Egypt in his time; his name refers to Buhut in the Gharbiyya region of Egypt. The library description says his Sharh Muntaha al-Iradat, also named Daqa'iq Uli al-Nuha li-Sharh al-Muntaha, is one of the commentaries relied on by the later Hanbalis. In it he explains Muntaha al-Iradat by Ibn al-Najjar al-Futuhi (died 972 AH). The description says Ibn al-Najjar's short text joined al-Muqni' of Ibn Qudama with al-Tanqih al-Mushbi' of al-Mardawi, adding some further points and showing the correct and preferred view acted on in the school, and that al-Buhuti then wrote his commentary by summarising from Ibn al-Najjar's own commentary and from his own commentary on al-Iqna'. The contents list includes the Book of Sale (Kitab al-Bay'), Interdiction (al-Hajr), Partnership (al-Sharikah), Loan for Use (al-Ariyah) and Endowment (al-Waqf). Source: book description and contents list of the Alam al-Kutub, Beirut edition (1993, three parts), as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.significance: Hanafi commentary on Hidayah.
rows.detail_long: Kamal al-Din Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahid, known as Ibn al-Humam (790-861 AH, 1388-1457 CE), was a Hanafi scholar whose family came from Sivas. He was born in Alexandria, made his name in Cairo, lived for a time in Aleppo and near the two Holy Mosques, and died in Cairo. Fath al-Qadir is his commentary on al-Hidayah of al-Marghinani; the library description introduces the Hidayah as the best-known book and most important short manual of Hanafi law. In the printed edition the text of the Hidayah stands at the top of each page, followed, below a dividing line, by Ibn al-Humam's commentary. The edition card says his commentary fills parts 1 to 7, and that the completion, titled Nata'ij al-Afkar, in parts 8 to 10, is published separately. The contents list includes the Book of Partnership (Kitab al-Sharikah), Endowment (al-Waqf), Sales (al-Buyu'), Currency Exchange (al-Sarf), Guarantee (al-Kafalah) and Transfer of Debt (al-Hawalah). Source: edition card, description and contents list of the Mustafa al-Babi al-Halabi, Egypt edition (1970), as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.significance: Legal maxims (qawa'id fiqhiyyah).
rows.detail_long: Two different books carry the title al-Ashbah wa al-Naza'ir. The first is by Jalal al-Din Abd al-Rahman al-Suyuti (849-911 AH, 1445-1505 CE), an imam, hadith master and historian with about 600 works, who grew up an orphan in Cairo. The library record classes his book under legal maxims in the Shafi'i school. Its description says he begins by explaining the five basic maxims to which scholars say all questions of law go back; the second book gives forty general maxims and the third twenty disputed ones; the fourth covers rulings that come up often, such as those of the one who forgets or is forced; and the later books cover parallels arranged by the chapters of fiqh and the differences between similar chapters. The second is by Zayn al-Din ibn Ibrahim, known as Ibn Nujaym (died 970 AH, 1563 CE), written on the school of Abu Hanifa. Its contents list is divided into seven 'arts', beginning with General Maxims (al-Qawa'id al-Kulliyyah) and including one on Devices (al-Hiyal) and one on Distinctions (al-Furuq). Source: descriptions and contents lists of the Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya editions (al-Suyuti 1983, Ibn Nujaym 1999), as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.significance: Standard practitioner text.
rows.detail_long: Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani writes in his foreword that he has served as chairman or member of the Shari'ah Supervisory Boards of a number of Islamic banks in different parts of the world, and that there he came across weaknesses in their operations caused mainly by the lack of a clear view of the relevant rules of Shari'ah. He describes An Introduction to Islamic Finance as a revised collection of his articles giving basic information on the principles of Islamic finance, with special reference to the modes of financing used by Islamic banks and non-banking financial institutions. He says he has tried to explain the concept behind each instrument, the requirements for its acceptance in Shari'ah and the correct way to apply it, in a simple way for the common reader. The foreword says that profit-and-loss sharing through musharakah and mudarabah is the basis for commercial financing, and that murabahah, ijarah, salam and istisna' are not substitutes for interest in the strict sense and have their own conditions. Chapter headings in the contents list include Musharakah, Mudarabah, Diminishing Musharakah, Murabahah, Ijarah, Salam, Islamic Investment Funds and The Principle of Limited Liability. Source: foreword and contents list of the book (title page: Quranic Studies Publishers, Maktaba Ma'ariful Qur'an), read in the Internet Archive full-text view.

rows.detail_long: Iqtisaduna (Our Economics) is by Sayyid Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr. In his foreword to the first edition the author sets out the plan of the book. He says the first chapter deals with the Marxist doctrine, examining historical materialism and then criticising the doctrine. The second chapter is devoted to the study and criticism of capitalism and its relationship with economics. The study of Islamic economics begins in the third chapter, which discusses a number of its basic ideas before moving to the details of the system. In the same foreword he speaks of the rights Islam gives to each element in the distribution of wealth and income according to the principles of lease, passive partnership, musaqat, muzara'ah, sale and loan. The contents list of the first part shows Chapter 1, Marxism, The Theory of Historical Materialism, and Chapter 2, Marxism and the Marxist Creed. rows.significance: Critical riba reassessment.
rows.detail_long: Abdullah Saeed's Islamic Banking and Interest carries the subtitle A Study of the Prohibition of Riba and its Contemporary Interpretation. In the acknowledgments the author thanks the University of Melbourne for the postgraduate scholarship under which the study was completed and for funds to collect data in Egypt, Jordan, the UK and Pakistan. He calls the study an initial attempt to question the validity of the interpretation of riba that Islamic banking rests on and the claims made for its successful implementation, and an attempt to highlight the moral and humanitarian emphasis given to riba in the Qur'an and Sunnah. The table of contents runs from the development of Islamic banks, through riba in the Qur'an, Sunnah and fiqh and the interpretation of riba in the modern period, to chapters on profit and loss sharing (mudaraba and musharaka), the murabaha financing mechanism, deposits and depositors, religious supervisory boards, and the 'Islamicity' of Islamic banking, which includes a critique of the neo-Revivalist interpretation of riba. Source: title page, acknowledgments, table of contents and conclusion of the book, read in the Internet Archive full-text view.

rows.detail_long: Wahbah ibn Mustafa al-Zuhayli was born in 1932 in the town of Dayr Atiyyah near Damascus. He studied at the Faculty of Shari'ah of al-Azhar, where he came first in 1956, and took a law degree from Ain Shams University in 1957. The edition card describes him as professor and head of the department of Islamic jurisprudence and its principles at the Faculty of Shari'ah, University of Damascus. The full title of al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuhu adds that it covers the legal evidence, the opinions of the schools, the most important juristic theories, and the checking and sourcing of the Prophet's hadith. The library description says the book was distributed across the Islamic world and translated into other languages such as Turkish, Malay and Persian. The contents list divides it into six sections: acts of worship; juristic theories; contracts or civil financial dealings (al-'Uqud aw al-Tasarrufat al-Madaniyyah al-Maliyyah); ownership and what follows from it; public law; and personal status. Source: edition card, description and contents list of the Dar al-Fikr, Damascus edition (fourth edition, eleven parts), with the author note, as shown in al-Maktaba al-Shamela.

rows.significance: Islamic monetary theory.
rows.detail_long: Muhammad Umer Chapra is introduced in the foreword by Khurshid Ahmad as an eminent economist and a committed Islamic scholar who, for the nineteen years before the book appeared, had worked as Economic Adviser to the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency, with monetary economics as his specialisation. Towards a Just Monetary System is subtitled a discussion of money, banking and monetary policy in the light of Islamic teachings, and was presented in the Islamic Economics Series of the Islamic Foundation, Leicester; the foreword is dated August 1984. The contents list moves from the goals and strategy of an Islamic monetary system to The Nature of Riba (chapter 2), The Alternative, which covers equity financing (chapter 3), Some Fundamental Reforms (chapter 4), Objections and Rationale (chapter 5), Institutional Setting, covering the central bank and commercial banks (chapter 6), Evaluation (chapter 8) and The Transition (chapter 9). An appendix sets out riba in the Qur'an, hadith and fiqh. The foreword calls the book a pioneering work. Source: title page, foreword and contents list of the Islamic Foundation edition, read in the Internet Archive full-text view.

rows.significance: Leading critical analysis.
rows.detail_long: Mahmoud A. El-Gamal is listed by the publisher as being at Rice University, Houston. The publisher's description says Islamic Finance: Law, Economics, and Practice gives an overview of the practice of Islamic finance and the historical roots that define its modes of operation, and that its focus is analytical and forward-looking. It says the book shows that Islamic finance exists mainly as a form of rent-seeking legal arbitrage: in every aspect of finance it aims to replicate in Islamic forms the substantive functions of contemporary financial instruments, markets and institutions. The description adds that, by doing this with pre-modern contract forms, Islamic finance has arguably failed to serve the objectives of Islamic law, and that the book proposes refocusing it on substance rather than form, with emphasis on community banking, micro-finance and socially responsible investment. Chapter titles include Jurisprudence and Arbitrage; Two Major Prohibitions: Riba and Gharar; Sale-Based Islamic Finance; Leasing, Securitization, and Sukuk; Partnerships and Equity Investment; Islamic Financial Institutions; Governance and Regulatory Solutions in Mutuality; and Beyond Shari'a Arbitrage. Source: publisher's description and contents list, Cambridge University Press (Cambridge Core).

rows.significance: Critique of Islamic economics.
rows.detail_long: Islam and Mammon is by Timur Kuran and is published by Princeton University Press. The catalogue description says the doctrine of 'Islamic economics' entered debates over the social role of Islam in the mid-twentieth century and has since pursued the goal of restructuring economies according to perceived Islamic teachings; beyond its most visible practical achievement, the establishment of Islamic banks meant to avoid interest, it has promoted Islamic norms of economic behaviour and founded redistribution systems modelled on early Islamic fiscal practices. According to the description, Kuran argues that the doctrine is simplistic, incoherent and largely irrelevant to present economic challenges, and finds that its practical applications have had no discernible effects on efficiency, growth or poverty reduction. His answer to why it has had any appeal is that its real purpose has been to cultivate a distinct Islamic identity to resist cultural globalization. The description adds that the Islamic sub-economies across the Islamic world emerged to meet the economic aspirations of socially marginalized groups, and that the book explores links between Islam and economic performance. Source: catalogue description of the Princeton University Press edition, Open Library.

rows.significance: Institutional-economics history.
rows.detail_long: The Long Divergence is by Timur Kuran and is published by Princeton University Press. The jacket description quoted in the catalogue calls the author one of the world's leading experts on Islamic economic institutions and the economy of the Middle East. It says that in the year 1000 the economy of the Middle East was at least as advanced as that of Europe, but that by 1800 the region had fallen dramatically behind in living standards, technology and economic institutions. According to the description, Kuran argues that what slowed development was not colonialism or geography, still less Muslim attitudes or some incompatibility between Islam and capitalism. Rather, starting around the tenth century, Islamic legal institutions that had benefited the Middle Eastern economy in the early centuries of Islam began to act as a drag on development, slowing or blocking the emergence of private capital accumulation, corporations, large-scale production and impersonal exchange. Source: jacket description of the Princeton University Press edition as quoted in the Open Library catalogue.

rows.title_original: Meezan Bank's Guide to Islamic Banking
rows.title_english: Meezan Bank's Guide to Islamic Banking
rows.significance: Practitioner product guide.
rows.detail_long: The title page of Meezan Bank's Guide to Islamic Banking says it was written by Dr. Muhammad Imran Ashraf Usmani, with assistance in translation, editing and compilation by Zeenat Zubairi, and published by Darul-Ishaat, Karachi, in a first edition of 2002. The preface argues that economic justice requires a viable economic system supported by an efficient banking system. The table of contents is set out in sections. Section I introduces the Islamic economic system, including the factors of production and the objectives of the distribution of wealth in Islam. Section II covers riba, its prohibition and classifications, with chapters on riba in the Qur'an and in hadith. Later sections cover the Islamic contract and sale, and the Islamic modes of financing, with a chapter each on Musharakah, Mudarabah, Diminishing Musharakah, Murabaha, Salam, Istisna', Istijrar, Ijarah (leasing) and Ijarah wa Iqtina. The closing sections cover banking in Islam, applications of Islamic financing (project, working capital, import and export financing) and Islamic investments, including securitization and Islamic investment funds. Source: title page, preface and table of contents of the Darul-Ishaat first edition, read in the Internet Archive full-text view.

rows.significance: Field-defining anthology.
rows.detail_long: Studies in Islamic Economics was edited by Khurshid Ahmad, who is named as Professor Khurshid Ahmad, chairman of the volume's editorial board. The title page describes it as a selection of papers presented to the First International Conference on Islamic Economics, held at Makka under the auspices of King Abdul Aziz University, Jeddah, on 21-26 February 1976. The contents list has two parts. Part I, Contributions to Islamic Economics, includes Islamic Economics: An Approach to Human Welfare by Dr. Anas Zarqa, a paper on the theory of consumer behaviour in an Islamic society by Dr. Monzer Kahf, Some Conceptual and Practical Aspects of Interest-Free Banking by Dr. Muhammad Uzair, Money, Interest and Qirad by Dr. Mahmud Abu Saud, Zakat and Fiscal Policy by Dr. F. R. Faridi, The Islamic Welfare State and its Role in the Economy by Dr. M. Umar Chapra, and Economic Development in an Islamic Framework by Khurshid Ahmad. Part II, Surveys on Islamic Economics, includes Muslim Economic Thinking: A Survey of Contemporary Literature by Dr. Muhammad Nejatullah Siddiqi. The appendices give the conference communique, participants and programme. Source: title page and contents list of the book, read in the Internet Archive full-text view.

rows.detail_long: Theoretical Studies in Islamic Banking and Finance was edited by Mohsin S. Khan and Abbas Mirakhor. The note says the institute hopes the series will make the principles of Islamic economics more widely understood and stimulate research in the field. The contents list gives nine papers: The Framework and Practice of Islamic Banking (Khan and Mirakhor); Islamic Interest-Free Banking: A Theoretical Analysis (Khan); The Relative Efficiency of Interest-Free Monetary Economies: The Fiat Money Case (Mabid Ali Al-Jarhi); Towards an Interest-Free Islamic Economic System (Waqar Masood Khan); An Economic Analysis of a PLS Model for the Financial Sector (Shahrukh Rafi Khan); Saving Behavior in an Economy Without Fixed Interest and Optimal Profit-Sharing Contracts and Investment in an Interest-Free Economy (Nadeem Ul Haque and Mirakhor); The Financial System and Monetary Policy in an Islamic Economy (Khan and Mirakhor); and Short-Term Asset Concentration and Islamic Banking (Mirakhor). Source: title page, contents list and institute's note of the book, read in the Internet Archive full-text view.

rows.significance: Early systematic textbook.
rows.detail_long: Islamic Economics: Theory and Practice is by M. A. Mannan and is subtitled A Comparative Study; it carries a foreword by Dr Charles S. Benson of the University of California. In his preface the author says the book seeks to give readers an insight into the economic values of Islam in the context of modern economic thought and is therefore primarily analytical. He says he tries to examine whether Islam could give a workable code of conduct and a blueprint of the socio-economic framework, and that he adds practical suggestions for policy, such as founding a Muslim World Bank, setting up consumers' co-operatives and establishing a People's Zakat Trust. He also says he discusses many economic problems of Pakistan in the light of Islamic values. The contents list begins with a chapter on Islamic economics, its meaning and scope, followed by chapters on Islamic and economic laws, Islam and other economic systems (capitalism, socialism, communism and fascism), consumption and production in Islam, and the factors of production. Source: title page, preface and contents list of the book, read in the Internet Archive full-text view.

rows.significance: Pre-modern riba treatise.
rows.detail_long: The title page of Islam and the Theory of Interest names its author as Anwar Iqbal Qureshi, head of the economics department at Osmania University and Economic Adviser to the government of H. E. H. the Nizam. The book carries a foreword by Professor Gyanchand, head of the economics department at Patna University, and an introduction by Allama Syed Sulaiman Nadvi, and was published by Shaikh Muhammad Ashraf, Kashmiri Bazar, Lahore. The contents list has four chapters. Chapter I, Western Theories of Interest, surveys Greek, Roman and medieval views, the classical, abstinence, productivity, Austrian and monetary theories, and Keynes on interest. Chapter II, The Islamic Theory of Interest, includes sections on the difference between trade and usury, types of riba, the orders on riba in the traditions of the Prophet, works of fiqh on interest, Islam and credit, and Islamic teachings on forward transactions. Chapter III is titled Interest-Usury, and Chapter IV, Islam and Prohibition of Banking Business, includes a section on the place of banks in the Islamic system. Source: title page and contents list of the Shaikh Muhammad Ashraf, Lahore edition, read in the Internet Archive full-text view (Digital Library of India scan).

rows.significance: Early policy critique.
rows.detail_long: Issues in Islamic Banking: Selected Papers is by Muhammad Nejatullah Siddiqi, with a foreword by Khurshid Ahmad. The foreword says that over the previous decade Dr. Siddiqi had written extensively on aspects of Islamic banking, mainly as papers contributed to international conferences and seminars on Islamic economics, and that he compiled these papers and lectures to form this book. The acknowledgements thank the International Centre for Research in Islamic Economics at King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, where two of the papers were first published or presented, in 1981 and at a seminar in Makka in 1977. The contents list includes Islamic Approaches to Money, Banking and Monetary Policy, with a postscript reviewing contributions during 1977-1981; Banking in an Islamic Framework; Rationale of Islamic Banking; Economics of Profit-Sharing; and Issues in Islamisation of Banking, which treats profit-sharing as the chief alternative to interest. Source: title page, acknowledgements, foreword and contents list of the book, read in the Internet Archive full-text view.

rows.title_original: Islamic Finance in the Global Economy
rows.title_english: Islamic Finance in the Global Economy
rows.significance: Political-economy survey.
rows.detail_long: Ibrahim Warde is Adjunct Professor of International Business at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy, Tufts University, according to the publisher's author note. The publisher's description says Islamic Finance in the Global Economy explains the paradox of a system rooted in the medieval era thriving in the global economy. It defines Islamic finance in its broadest sense to include banks, mutual funds, securities firms and insurance (takaful) companies, places it in the context of the global political and economic system, and covers its underlying principles, its range of products and country differences, along with economic, political, regulatory and religious concerns. The description says the second edition was completely revised and updated. Chapter titles include Islamic Finance in Theory and Practice; Riba, Gharar, and the Moral Economy of Islam in Historical and Comparative Perspective; The Evolution of Modern Islamic Finance; Country Differences; Financial Products and Instruments; Regulatory Issues and Challenges: Global Norms and Religious Constraints; and Religious Issues and Challenges: Defining Islam and Interpreting the Shariah. Source: publisher's description, contents list and author note for the second edition (2010), Edinburgh University Press.

rows.significance: Comprehensive practitioner text.
rows.detail_long: Muhammad Ayub is described in the publisher's author note as Director of Training, Development and Shari'ah Aspects at IIBI, London, and formerly with the State Bank of Pakistan, the central bank, where he headed the Islamic Economics Division and the Shari'ah Compliance Division. The publisher's description says that in Understanding Islamic Finance he introduces the essential elements of this growing market, giving an in-depth background to the subject and clear descriptions of the major products and processes associated with Islamic finance. The key features it lists are a discussion of the principles of Islamic finance; an introduction to the key products and procedures that international financial institutions use or may adopt to fund clients in a Shari'ah-compliant way; a discussion of the role Islamic finance can play in the development of the financial system and of economies; and practical examples covering deposit and fund management by banks, risk management, accounting treatment, and the working of Islamic financial markets and instruments. The publisher presents it as a text for banks and financial institutions entering this market and for undergraduate and postgraduate students of Islamic finance. Source: publisher's description and author note, John Wiley & Sons (2007, 544 pages, Wiley Finance Series).

The publisher's description of Product Development in Islamic Banks says that while other texts discuss the basic principles and contracts used in Islamic banking and finance, few discuss how these can be used to develop financial products. It says the book fills that gap, starting with the basic principles that form the building blocks of contemporary Islamic financial products and then discussing the more intricate issues of product development processes. The key features listed include identifying three phases of the product development cycle and making suggestions for the future direction of the Islamic financial industry. Chapter titles include Islamic Law and Finance: Concepts and Principles; Innovation and Product Development: Strategy, Structure and Process; Product Development Practices in Islamic Banks; Islamic Financial Products: Categories and Controversies; and Shari'ah Based Islamic Finance: The Way Forward. Source: publisher's description, contents list and author note, Edinburgh University Press (Edinburgh Guides to Islamic Finance, 2011).

rows.title_original: Risk Sharing in Finance: The Islamic Finance Alternative
rows.significance: Risk-sharing thesis (Wiley); co-authors Askari, Krichene, Mirakhor (S026)
rows.note: named in source doc under Zamir Iqbal
rows.detail_long: Risk Sharing in Finance: The Islamic Finance Alternative is listed in a library catalogue under four authors: Hossein Askari, Zamir Iqbal, Noureddine Krichene and Abbas Mirakhor. It was published in Singapore by John Wiley & Sons (Asia). The description on the library record says the financial crisis of 2008 led a number of academics, practitioners and policymakers to question the fundamental stability of the conventional financial system, a system predominantly based on debt financing and leveraging. It presents as an alternative a system with no debt financing, only equity or direct asset financing, in which there would be no 'risk shifting' as happens with debt, only 'risk sharing' as happens with equity or asset financing. The description says such a system has been suggested by a number of noted conventional economists over the last hundred years, and that its basic principles have been advocated by Islam and to some extent by other Abrahamic religions. It adds the authors' view that much of the rapid growth in the practice of Islamic finance has been superficial. Source: description on the Internet Archive catalogue record for the John Wiley & Sons (Asia) edition, with the author list from the Open Library record.

rows.detail_long: This is an edited volume. The publisher lists its editors as Ahmed Belouafi, Abderrazak Belabes and Cristina Trullols; Belouafi and Belabes are shown at the Islamic Economics Institute of King Abdulaziz University, Saudi Arabia, and Trullols at IE Business School, Spain. The publisher describes the book as the first of its kind in covering the developments and prospects of Islamic finance education in Western higher education, intended as a reference for academics and researchers, and says it gives an insight into ethics and values in curricula development at business schools and in finance departments. It has 22 chapters. After an introduction by the three editors, a part headed "Islamic Finance Higher Education: Cartography" includes chapters such as "Islamic Finance Higher Education at a Glance: A Global Picture", "Islamic Finance Education in the UK: Opportunities and Challenges", "Islamic Finance Education in France: An Unexpected Surge" and "Islamic Finance Education at the Top Ten Business Schools". A second part, "Islamic Finance Higher Education in the West: Cases and Experiments", has chapters on single institutions, among them Henley Business School at Reading University, La Trobe University, Newcastle University, Bangor University and the Markfield Institute of Higher Education. It was published by Palgrave Macmillan in 2012 in the IE Business Publishing series. Source: publisher's description and table of contents, Palgrave Macmillan book page on Springer Nature Link.

rows.title_original: The Islamic Economy: Analytical Study of the Functioning of the Islamic Economic System
rows.significance: Kahf's early systemic study
rows.detail_long: Monzer Kahf's own curriculum vitae lists him as a consultant, trainer and lecturer in Islamic banking, finance and economics in private practice in California since 1999, a former research economist at the Islamic Research and Training Institute of the Islamic Development Bank in Jeddah, and a professor of Islamic economics and banking at Yarmouk University, Jordan, in 2004-2005. His publication list gives this book as published in Plainfield, Indiana, by the Muslim Students' Association of the United States and Canada in 1978. The introduction is headed "The Need for a General Theory of the Islamic Economy". Kahf writes there that existing works explain the essential principles of the economic system in Islam but that there is little on the mechanism of the functioning of this system, and that his study attempts to fill this gap. He says the study does not occupy itself with the legal and ideological justification of the Islamic teachings in economics but investigates their economic significance and implications, showing how such an economy works and how variables such as investment, savings and consumption are determined. The book has six chapters: Chapter One introduces Islamic economics and its methodology, Chapters Two and Three deal with consumption and production theories, Chapter Four investigates the market structure, and Chapters Five and Six construct the macroeconomic model and study its policy implications. Source: the book's own introduction (full-text view, Internet Archive) and the author's own website.

rows.significance: Chapra's maqasid-development thesis (IRTI open access)
rows.detail_long: The publisher describes Muhammad Umer Chapra as Research Advisor at the Islamic Research and Training Institute of the Islamic Development Bank, Jeddah, who earlier worked at the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency in Riyadh for nearly 35 years, retiring as Senior Economic Advisor, and who taught economics at the University of Wisconsin (Platteville) and the University of Kentucky. This 56-page paper, published in 2008, explores the Islamic vision of development in relation to the maqasid al-shari'ah, which the publisher glosses as the higher intents and purposes of Islamic law. The description says the purpose of the Shari'ah, as recognised by almost all the jurists, is to serve the interests of all human beings and to save them from harm. Chapra argues that Islam has emphasised all the ingredients of human well-being, including the human self, faith, intellect, posterity and wealth, for society to flourish. The description adds that for the Muslim world to focus on economic development only may bring higher growth in the short term but in the long run will lead to a rise in inequities, family disintegration, juvenile delinquency, crime and social unrest. The Islamic Development Bank Institute lists the same title as a 2008 research paper under the subject Shari'ah. Source: publisher's description and author note, International Institute of Islamic Thought; catalogue entry, Islamic Development Bank Institute.

rows.title_original: The Text of the Historic Judgment on Interest
rows.url_checked: 2026-11-26: opened twice (second read independent). A republication of the judgment text (not the court or the first publisher).
rows.significance: Pakistan Supreme Court Shariat Appellate Bench riba judgment (delivered 23 Dec 1999), Usmani's section
rows.detail_long: A library author card describes Muhammad Taqi Usmani as a Shari'ah appellate judge at the Supreme Court of Pakistan and vice-president of the Islamic Fiqh Academy in Jeddah, born in Deoband in 1943. This text is his judgment in a group of appeals, heard together, against a Federal Shariat Court judgment of 14 November 1991 that had declared a number of the country's laws repugnant to the injunctions of Islam because they provided for charging or paying interest. Appellants argued that modern interest-based commercial transactions are not covered by the Qur'anic term riba, a view supported before the court by five different lines of argument, which the judgment examines. Its sections include "An Objective Study of the Quranic Verses Dealing with Riba", "What is Meant by Riba?", "Productive or Consumption Loans", "Rationale of the Prohibition of Riba", "Nature of Money", "Interest and Indexation", "Mark-Up and Interest", "Riba and Doctrine of Necessity", "Profit and Loss Sharing" and "Murabaha Transaction". The conclusions state that any additional amount over the principal in a contract of loan or debt is the riba prohibited by the Qur'an, and that there is no difference between different types of loans so far as the prohibition is concerned. The judgment ends by dismissing all the appeals. Source: English text of the judgment as published by SeekersGuidance; author details from the al-Maktaba al-Shamela author card.

rows.title_original: Thirty Years of Islamic Banking: History, Performance and Prospects
rows.significance: Standard industry history (Palgrave)
rows.detail_long: The publisher lists the authors as Munawar Iqbal and Philip Molyneux; a research-papers index gives their affiliations as the Islamic Development Bank and the University of Wales. The publisher's author note describes Molyneux as Professor of Banking and Finance at Bangor University, UK, whose main area of research is the structure and efficiency of banking markets. According to the publisher, the text explains how Islamic banking works and what it offers as an alternative model of financial intermediation. The questions it addresses include why Islamic banking started and where it is going, who the main players are, what its strengths and weaknesses are, whether Islamic banks will survive in highly competitive and globalised financial markets, and how their performance and efficiency compare with conventional banks. Its ten chapters include "Theoretical Foundations of Islamic Banking", "Development of the Islamic Banking Model", "History and Growth of Islamic Banking and Finance", "The Performance of Islamic Banks", "Efficiency in Islamic Banking", "Challenges Facing Islamic Banking" and "Islamic Banking in the Twenty-First Century". It was published by Palgrave Macmillan in the series Palgrave Macmillan Studies in Banking and Financial Institutions, with a 2005 copyright date. Source: publisher's description, Palgrave Macmillan book page on Springer Nature Link; chapter list, RePEc/IDEAS record.

rows.title_original: Islamic Law and Finance: Religion, Risk, and Return
rows.significance: Canonical Western legal-finance study (Kluwer)
rows.detail_long: A Harvard Magazine notice of this book identifies Samuel Hayes III as Schiff professor of investment banking and Frank Vogel as the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques assistant professor of Islamic legal studies. It says that in the book the two authors explore how the Qur'an shapes Islamic finance, against the background of the Qur'an's prohibition on interest-taking (riba) and speculation (gharar). The notice quotes Vogel as saying that the bulk of Islamic transactions are short-term, low-risk inventory markup deals called murabaha. It also quotes his view that demands for more than nominal practices are stimulating innovations that promise to make Islamic finance more robust and in step with the requirements of modern commerce. A library catalogue record gives the publisher as Kluwer Law International, with a 1998 copyright date, in the Arab and Islamic Laws Series, number 16. Source: Harvard Magazine notice of the book (1998); catalogue record, CiNii Books.

rows.detail_long: A library author card gives the author as Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani (131-189 AH, 748-804 CE), a leading authority in law and legal theory and the one who spread the learning of Abu Hanifa. The same card explains that his work al-Mabsut is also called al-Asl because it is the foundation of his books and the most extensive of them. Alongside books on prayer, zakat and fasting, the contents list includes the Book of Sales and Salam, the Book of Currency Exchange (sarf), the Book of Pledge, the Book of Hire, the Book of Partnership and the Book of Mudaraba, and also a Book of Kharaj. rows.detail_long: A library author card describes Ibn Khaldun (732-808 AH, 1332-1406 CE), 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad, as a philosopher, historian and social scientist whose family came from Seville and who was born and raised in Tunis. It says he later went to Egypt, where he held the Maliki judgeship, and that he died in Cairo. The card says he is famous for his history, the Kitab al-'Ibar, the first part of which is the Muqaddimah, and that the Muqaddimah is counted among the foundations of sociology. The library's note on the work says that in the Muqaddimah he laid down the principles of the understanding of history and of the science of civilisation ('ilm al-'umran), and gives its subject as inquiry into the causes of the collapse and flourishing of states. The note adds that he first completed it in five months in 779 AH while staying at Qal'at Bani Salama, and afterwards revised it. The edition described is the Dar al-Fikr, Beirut, printing of the whole history in eight volumes (1981), with the text prepared by Khalil Shahada and reviewed by Suhayl Zakkar. Source: book card and author card, al-Maktaba al-Shamela (Dar al-Fikr edition).

rows.detail_long: The library card gives the author as Zayn al-Din ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhammad, known as Ibn Nujaym, who died in 970 AH (1563 CE). The library's author card describes him simply as one of the scholars, with written works that include al-Ashbah wa-l-Naza'ir, al-Bahr al-Ra'iq (a commentary on Kanz al-Daqa'iq) and collections of treatises and fatwas. The full title of this book is al-Ashbah wa-l-Naza'ir according to the school of Abu Hanifa al-Nu'man. After an introduction it is divided into seven "arts": the first on universal maxims (al-qawa'id al-kulliyya), the second on useful points, the third on joining and distinguishing, the fourth on riddles, the fifth on legal devices (hiyal), the sixth on distinctions, and the seventh on anecdotes and correspondence. The edition described has notes and hadith references by Shaykh Zakariyya 'Umayrat and was published by Dar al-Kutub al-'Ilmiyya, Beirut, in 1999 in 373 pages. Source: book card, contents list and author card, al-Maktaba al-Shamela (Dar al-Kutub al-'Ilmiyya edition).

rows.title_english: The Answer to the Perplexed (Ibn Abidin's Gloss)
rows.url_checked: 2026-11-26: opened twice (second read independent). Arabic text (Shamela).
rows.significance: Late-Hanafi authority most cited in modern finance fatwas
rows.detail_long: A library author card gives the author as Muhammad Amin ibn 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz 'Abidin of Damascus, known as Ibn 'Abidin (1198-1252 AH, 1784-1836 CE), and calls him the jurist of the Syrian lands and the leading Hanafi of his age, born and died in Damascus. The library's note on the book classes it as Hanafi law. It explains that the work is a gloss on al-Durr al-Mukhtar of al-Haskafi (died 1088 AH), which is itself a commentary on Tanwir al-Absar of al-Timirtashi (died 1004 AH), so that the gloss gathers the efforts of three scholars. The note says Ibn 'Abidin died before finishing it and that his son, Shaykh Muhammad 'Ala' al-Din, completed it in two volumes titled Qurrat 'Uyun al-Akhyar. The contents include the Book of Partnership, the Book of Waqf, the Book of Sales, the Book of Suretyship (kafala) and the Book of Debt Transfer (hawala). The library's note calls it, without qualification, the most important book among the later Hanafis, marked by its setting out of rulings for questions that arose in later ages, and says the gloss became the reliance of jurists, judges and muftis. Source: book card, contents list and author card, al-Maktaba al-Shamela (Mustafa al-Babi al-Halabi edition, Cairo, 1966).

rows.title_original: Islam's Solution of the Basic Economic Problems
rows.title_english: Islam's Solution of the Basic Economic Problems
rows.significance: Hamidullah's pioneering article (Islamic Culture) — among the earliest modern Islamic-economics writings
rows.detail_long: A research-archive abstract describes Dr. Muhammad Hamidullah as famous for his French translation of the Qur'an and acknowledged for his research on international Islamic law, the biography of the Prophet, Islamic politics and the archival heritage of Islam. The same abstract calls his works on Islamic economics pioneering and says it was he who coined the term "Islamic Economics". A second abstract, for a volume of his collected papers, says he started his writings on Islamic economics in the 1930s. A bibliography entry gives this article under the fuller title "Islam's Solution of the Basic Economic Problems--the Position of Labour", published in the journal Islamic Culture, volume 10, number 2, 1936, pages 213-33. Source: abstracts, Munich Personal RePEc Archive; bibliography entry, On Work.

rows.significance: Fazlur Rahman's modernist reinterpretation (Islamic Studies, Karachi)
rows.detail_long: The article is headed with the author's name, Fazlur Rahman, and appeared in the journal Islamic Studies (Islamabad), volume 3, number 1, 1964. An editor's note says it is a translation by Mazheruddin Siddiqi of an Urdu article by the author that was published in November 1963 in Fikr-o-Nazar, the monthly Urdu journal of the same institute. In an opening note the author says riba is usually translated in Urdu by the word sud, that sud is not synonymous with the Qur'anic term riba, and that any attempt to translate the Qur'anic term in any language is futile and a source of much confused thinking on the subject. The introduction sets out the literal meanings of riba as illustrated by Qur'anic usage, such as to grow, to increase and to rise. The author then gives his plan: first to take up the nature of the riba prohibited by the Qur'an, and in a second section to turn to the legal hadith materials concerning the extension of the Qur'anic term to different forms of exchange and transactions. Source: the article's own first pages, full-text view, Internet Archive.

rows.significance: Baqir al-Sadr's operational blueprint for interest-free banking (Shia tradition)
rows.detail_long: The library record gives the author as Muhammad Baqir Sadr and the title as al-Bank al-la-Ribawi fi al-Islam. The text opens with a section headed "Our position on the proposal". There the author says that, in trying to plan a proposal for an interest-free bank, a basic distinction must be drawn between two positions. The first is that of someone who plans an interest-free bank within a comprehensive plan for society. The second is that of someone who plans to set up an interest-free bank independently of the other sides of society, with other interest-based institutions, banks and others, remaining in place. He writes that this does not amount to an excuse for failing to apply the Shari'ah where that is possible, because every ruling of Islam must be applied in any case, whether or not the other rulings are applied. Source: opening pages of the text, OpenITI-derived copy, Internet Archive.

rows.title_english: The Theory of Maslaha in Islamic Jurisprudence
rows.significance: Hussain Hamid Hassan's doctoral work on public interest
rows.detail_long: The description attached to a library scan gives the title as Nazariyyat al-Maslaha fi al-Fiqh al-Islami, the author as Husayn Hamid Hassan, the publisher as Dar al-Nahda al-'Arabiyya and the year as 1971. It says the book studies the theory of maslaha (interest, benefit) in Islamic jurisprudence, the content of which is that the rulings brought by the texts of the Shari'ah secure the interests of people in this life and the next. According to the description, where a text gives a ruling on a specific case, that ruling is followed even if the jurist supposes the interest lies elsewhere. Where no specific text exists, the jurist must look for the ruling in the Shari'ah texts only, giving the case a ruling that secures an interest the texts themselves protect, or an interest of the same kind. The description says the theory rests on two foundations: the completeness of the Shari'ah and the sufficiency of its texts for the needs of the community, and that the Lawgiver intends by His law the interests of His servants. Source: uploader's description of the 1971 Dar al-Nahda al-'Arabiyya edition, Internet Archive.

rows.title_original: Economic Development in an Islamic Framework
rows.title_english: Economic Development in an Islamic Framework
rows.significance: Khurshid Ahmad's agenda-setting development paper (Leicester)
rows.detail_long: A journal index lists the author as Khursheed Ahmad and describes him as President of the Institute of Political Studies, Islamabad, Minister of Planning and Development, and Deputy Chairman of the Planning Committee, Pakistan. The record read is for an Arabic translation of the paper, under the English title "Economic development in an Islamic framework", translated by Rafiq Yunus al-Masri. Its abstract opens by saying that a great challenge faces the Muslim world: the challenge of rebuilding its economy in a way that fits its global intellectual, political and economic role. It asks whether this calls for economic development aimed at "catching up" with the industrial countries of the West, capitalist or socialist, or for a comprehensive social and economic reconstruction guided by an entirely different model, with its own assumptions, ideals and values. Source: abstract of the Arabic translation, RePEc/IDEAS record.

rows.significance: Islamic Foundation collection
rows.detail_long: The publisher lists this book as by M. Fahim Khan. It describes the work as a systematic and rigorous exposition of various aspects of the economics of Islam, and quotes John Presley, a former professor of economics at the University of Loughborough, calling it precisely the kind of book that Western economists have been waiting for. A library record gives the first edition as published in Leicester by the Islamic Foundation, with a 1995 copyright date, as number 19 in its Islamic Economics Series. The library's contents list has thirteen chapters. They begin with "Introduction: overview of an Islamic Economy" and "Theory of consumer behaviour in the Islamic Perspective", and go on to "An overview of the financial system of Islam", "The viability and economics of islamic banking" and "Time value of money and discounting in islamic perspective". The last chapter is "Practical considerations regarding the introduction of profit/loss-sharing (PLS) based financial system". Source: publisher's description, Kube Publishing (Islamic Foundation); table of contents, UniSZA library catalogue record.

rows.detail_long: The issuing body is the Islamic Fiqh Academy, which the publisher's catalogue names as author. The catalogue describes the volume as the resolutions and recommendations on different issues issued by the Council of the Islamic Fiqh Academy from its 2nd session to its 12th session. It was published in 2000 in the Islamic Economics Translations Series, a 269-page work in English filed under the subject Shari'ah. As an example of the kind of text involved, the Academy's own website carries Resolution Nos. 40-41 of its 5th session, held in Kuwait City on 10-15 December 1988, on keeping a promise and murabaha to the purchase orderer. That resolution states that murabaha to the purchase orderer is permissible on goods that are already in the physical possession of the seller, provided the seller carries the risk of loss before delivery. It also states that a unilateral promise is morally binding on the promisor unless there is a valid excuse. Source: publisher's catalogue description, Islamic Development Bank Institute; one resolution as published on the International Islamic Fiqh Academy website.

rows.title_english: Financial Transactions in Islamic Jurisprudence (trans. El-Gamal)
rows.significance: Zuhayli's transactions volume in English — bridges B029 to English readers; translator El-Gamal (S031)
rows.detail_long: The title page presents this as Dr. Wahbah al-Zuhayli's al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuh (Islamic Jurisprudence and Its Proofs), under the English title Financial Transactions in Islamic Jurisprudence, translated by Mahmoud A. El-Gamal and revised by Muhammad S. Eissa, with the copyright held by Dar al-Fikr, Damascus. In his preface the translator says the first volume is an English translation of Volume 5 of al-Zuhayli's work in its fourth edition of 1997, and that his goal was to give non-Arabic readers access to the rich Islamic juristic literature on financial transactions. He cautions that the translation is no more accessible than the Arabic original, because Islamic jurisprudence is a highly technical field, and explains that the author often sets out one jurist's opinion, then an opposing opinion, then the proofs of each. The work is arranged in parts by type of contract. Part headings in the first volume include "The Sales Contract", "Types of Sale", "The loan contract", "The Lease Contract", "Partnerships", "Silent Partnership (mudarabah)", "The Gift Contract" and "The Agency Contract". The first part opens with chapters on the constituents of sale and the conditions of sale. Source: title page, translator's preface and contents pages of the English translation, full-text view, Internet Archive.

rows.significance: Usmani's contemporary-transactions rulings (2 vols)
rows.note: Publication year varies by edition — verify
rows.detail_long: A library author card describes Muhammad Taqi Usmani, son of Mufti Muhammad Shafi', as a Shari'ah appellate judge at the Supreme Court of Pakistan and vice-president of the Islamic Fiqh Academy in Jeddah, born in Deoband in 1943. This book, whose title means studies in contemporary juristic issues, is a collection of his separate studies. After the author's foreword, the contents list includes studies on the rulings of sale by instalments, sale by mutual handing over (ta'ati) and istijrar, the sale of abstract rights, and commodity futures contracts in the light of the Islamic Shari'ah. It also has studies on the rulings of paper currency, on change in the value of currency and its linking to a price index, on muqarada bonds and investment bonds, on lawful methods of housing finance, and on the rulings of bank deposits, together with answers to enquiries from the Islamic Development Bank in Jeddah. A few studies deal with other subjects, such as traffic accidents and imported meat. The edition described is the second, published by Dar al-Qalam, Damascus, in 2003 in 456 pages. Source: book card, contents list and author card, al-Maktaba al-Shamela (Dar al-Qalam edition).

rows.significance: Kamali's accessible overview (Oneworld)
rows.detail_long: The publisher lists the author as Mohammad Hashim Kamali. It describes the book as a comprehensive and accessible examination of Shari'ah law that examines the sources, characteristic features and schools of thought of a system it says is often stereotyped in the West for its severity. According to the publisher, Kamali discusses, in a progressive and graduated fashion, topics ranging from juristic disagreement to independent reasoning. The description says he also broaches more advanced topics such as the principle of legality and the role and place of Shari'ah-oriented policy, and questions whether Islam is as much of a law-based religion as it has often been made out to be. The book has a bibliography and glossary, a general index and an index of Arabic quotations. It was published by Oneworld Publications on 17 March 2008 in the series The Foundations of Islam, in 352 pages. Source: publisher's description, Oneworld Publications.

rows.significance: Van Greuning & Zamir Iqbal (World Bank) — supervisory risk framework; open via World Bank
rows.detail_long: The record lists the authors as Zamir Iqbal and Hennie Van Greuning, and the publisher as the World Bank, 2008. Its abstract says the publication provides a comprehensive overview of topics related to the assessment, analysis and management of various types of risks in the field of Islamic banking. The abstract adds that the Islamic financial system is not limited to banking but also covers capital formation, capital markets and all types of financial intermediation and risk transfer. rows.significance: Daud Bakar & Engku Rabiah (eds), CERT — Malaysian practitioner canon
rows.detail_long: Library records give this book as edited by Mohd Daud Bakar and Engku Rabiah Adawiah Engku Ali and published in Kuala Lumpur by CERT Publications, with a 2008 copyright date, in xxi and 612 pages. The catalogue summary describes it as a collection of separately written papers that had been presented in various workshops and seminars, by authors who are prominent figures from different backgrounds. It says the book contains twenty-two papers falling under five themes: Shari'ah Framework of Islamic Banking and Finance; Islamic Banking Development; Takaful (Islamic Insurance); Legal, Accounting and Governance in Islamic Finance; and Islamic Capital Market. According to the summary, the book gives an overview of the practice of Islamic finance and highlights the latest developments in the industry, and some of the papers analyse the specific practicalities of contemporary financial instruments within the Shari'ah compliance framework. It also discusses the challenges faced by the Islamic finance industry and proposes suggestions for the way forward. Source: catalogue records and summary, UniSZA library (drawing on the International Islamic University Malaysia repository).

rows.detail_long: The publisher's author note describes Abbas Mirakhor as the First Holder of the INCEIF Chair in Islamic Finance at INCEIF, the Global University of Islamic Finance, Malaysia, a former Executive Director and Dean of the Executive Board of the International Monetary Fund, with a PhD from Kansas State University. It describes Hossein Askari as Iran Professor of International Business and International Affairs at George Washington University. According to the publisher, the book briefly surveys the evolution of the Western concept of development, recognising the wider dimensions of human and economic development and the role of institutions and rules, a concept which it says has moved toward the vision and the path of development envisaged in Islam. It has six chapters: "The Evolution of the Western Concept of Development", "Development as Human Well-being", "The Foundational Elements of Development in Islam", "The Dimensions of Development in Islam", "The Institutional Structure of Development in Islam" and "Conclusion". It was published by Palgrave Macmillan, New York, in 2010. Source: publisher's description, table of contents and author notes, Palgrave Macmillan book page on Springer Nature Link.

rows.title_original: What Is Wrong with Islamic Economics?
rows.title_english: What Is Wrong with Islamic Economics?
rows.significance: Akram Khan's insider critique (Edward Elgar)
rows.detail_long: The record lists the author as Muhammad Akram Khan and the publisher as Edward Elgar Publishing, 2013. Its abstract says the book takes an objective look at the state of the art in Islamic economics and finance, analyses reasons for perceived stagnation and also suggests a way forward. The chapters listed on the record begin with "Islamic economics: state of the art", "The 'why' of Islamic economics", "What is Islamic economics?" and "Methodology of Islamic economics", and include "An Islamic economic system or spiritual capitalism?". A long run of chapters deals with riba, among them "Prohibition of riba in the primary sources of Islam", "Theory of riba: the orthodox interpretation", "Modernist thinking on riba" and "Prohibition of riba: the way forward". Later chapters are "Theoretical basis of Islamic banking", "Problems of profit-loss sharing", "Practice of Islamic banking and finance", "A trajectory of legal tricks (hiyal)", "Islamic insurance (takaful)" and "Contemporary application of the law of zakah". Source: abstract and chapter list, RePEc/IDEAS record (Edward Elgar Publishing).

rows.title_original: Morality and Justice in Islamic Economics and Finance
rows.title_english: Morality and Justice in Islamic Economics and Finance
rows.url_checked: 2026-11-26: page opened and shows this book.
rows.significance: A 2014 collection of eight essays by M. Umer Chapra on Islamic economics and finance, with an introduction.
rows.detail_long: The record describes the book as an introduction followed by eight essays chosen from M. Umer Chapra's writing. The opening chapters deal with Islamic economics, starting with whether such a field is needed at all. One chapter applies Ibn Khaldun's ideas on development to present-day Muslim countries. The later chapters turn to finance: the argument against interest, new products and their authenticity, and the problems the industry faces. The last chapter offers proposals for reforming world finance after the crisis.

rows.detail_long: Wael B. Hallaq's book is presented by its publisher as a long account of how Islamic law developed over time. It has three parts, the first on the law before the modern period, from its formation to the later dynasties. The second part outlines the rules themselves, and its seventh chapter is the one on contracts. That part also has a chapter on property. The third part follows the changes brought by colonial rule and nation-states.
